title: Patterns everywhere
description:
Use pattern matching (slice patterns, ranges, `@` bindings, guards, `let else`) for each function:

```rust
fn shape_of(values: &[i32]) -> String
fn age_group(age: u32) -> String
fn parse_move(text: &str) -> Option<(char, u32)>
fn quadrant(point: (i32, i32)) -> &'static str
```

- `shape_of`: `"empty"`, `"single N"`, `"pair A B"`; for longer slices `"palindrome"` when it reads the same backwards (check the ends with a slice pattern, recursively), else `"N items from F to L"`.
- `age_group`: 0 to 12 `"child N"`, 13 to 19 `"teen N"`, 20 to 64 `"adult"`, 65 and over `"senior N"` (with the age bound by `@`).
- `parse_move`: text like `"N12"`, `"e3"` or `" S 4 "`: a direction letter (N, E, S, W, either case, returned in upper case) and a positive distance; spaces anywhere are ignored. Anything else is `None`. Use `let ... else`.
- `quadrant`: `"origin"`, `"x axis"`, `"y axis"`, or `"I"`, `"II"`, `"III"`, `"IV"` (counter-clockwise from top right).
hints: `[first, middle @ .., last]` binds the inner part of a slice to `middle`, which makes a recursive palindrome check one line.
`let Some(dir @ ('N' | 'E' | 'S' | 'W')) = ... else { return None };` matches, binds and checks the letter in one statement.

A few `char` and `Chars` helpers make `parse_move` short: `c.is_whitespace()` tests for a space, `c.to_ascii_uppercase()` turns `'e'` into `'E'`, and after `let mut chars = text.chars(); chars.next();` the call `chars.as_str()` gives the rest of the text as a `&str`, ready to `parse`.
